Optimal Execution Theory

Introduction¶

Chapter Execution fundamentals established the economic motivations and practical vocabulary of algorithmic execution: why large orders generate market impact, how different benchmarks measure execution quality, and how the tension between market impact and timing risk creates the trader’s dilemma. This chapter builds on that foundation by providing the mathematical theory that underlies optimal execution algorithms. The central question is: given a large order to execute over a fixed time horizon, what sequence of child order sizes minimises the expected cost of execution for a given level of risk tolerance?

Answering this question rigorously requires casting execution as an optimal control problem — a framework developed in chapter Stochastic Optimal Control. The agent’s state is the remaining inventory xtx_txt​, the control is the trading rate vtv_tvt​, and the cost functional combines expected market impact with the variance of the execution cost. The solution yields a complete characterisation of the efficient frontier of execution strategies, parametrised by risk aversion. This frontier generalises naturally to multiple assets traded simultaneously, where correlations between price movements allow natural hedging during execution.

The chapter is organised as follows. Section Designing execution algorithms formalises the execution problem as an optimal control problem, introducing the price dynamics, market impact model, and cost functional. Section The Almgren–Chriss model derives the Almgren–Chriss solution Almgren & Chriss, 2000: the optimal continuous-time trajectory, its efficient frontier, and its discrete-time implementation. Section Implementation Shortfall target discusses the IS algorithm and the connection to the Bertsimas–Lo result Bertsimas & Lo, 1998. Section VWAP target develops the theory of VWAP-optimal execution, from the static proportional schedule through the dynamic adaptation of Busseti & Boyd (2015). Section Portfolio execution extends the framework to portfolio execution with cross-asset impact and natural hedging.

Designing execution algorithms¶

The execution problem as an optimal control problem¶

Consider an agent who must buy (or sell) a total of X>0X > 0X>0 shares of an asset over a time horizon [0,T][0, T][0,T]. We formulate this as a continuous-time optimal control problem with state xtx_txt​ (remaining inventory) and control vtv_tvt​ (trading rate):

  • State variable: xtx_txt​ = number of shares still to be executed at time ttt, with x0=Xx_0 = Xx0​=X and the constraint xT=0x_T = 0xT​=0 (full execution by time TTT).

  • Control variable: vt≥0v_t \geq 0vt​≥0 = rate of execution (shares per unit time). The state evolves as

x˙t=−vt⇒xt=X−∫0tvs ds\dot{x}_t = -v_t \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad x_t = X - \int_0^t v_s \, dsx˙t​=−vt​⇒xt​=X−∫0t​vs​ds
(1)

so that the constraint xT=0x_T = 0xT​=0 is equivalent to ∫0Tvt dt=X\int_0^T v_t \, dt = X∫0T​vt​dt=X.

The trader is liquidating (selling) throughout, so vt≥0v_t \geq 0vt​≥0 and xtx_txt​ is non-increasing.

Price dynamics¶

Absent any trading, the mid-price StS_tSt​ follows a diffusion process. In the Almgren–Chriss framework Almgren & Chriss, 2000, the price is modelled as an arithmetic Brownian motion modified by the permanent market impact of the trader’s own activity:

dSt=σ dWt−g(vt) dtdS_t = \sigma \, dW_t - g(v_t) \, dtdSt​=σdWt​−g(vt​)dt
(2)

where σ>0\sigma > 0σ>0 is the price volatility (constant for simplicity), WtW_tWt​ is a standard Wiener process, and g(vt)≥0g(v_t) \geq 0g(vt​)≥0 is the permanent impact function — the irreversible price depression caused by the trader’s sell flow. The price process is a martingale in the absence of trading (vt=0v_t = 0vt​=0), consistent with the efficient market hypothesis, and is depressed by the accumulated permanent impact of all prior trading.

The choice g(v)=γvg(v) = \gamma vg(v)=γv (linear permanent impact) is the primary tractable case, yielding a clean closed-form solution. More general impact functions can be handled variationally but typically require numerical methods.

Linear market impact model¶

When vtv_tvt​ shares are sold per unit time, the actual execution price received for each share is not StS_tSt​ but StS_tSt​ adjusted downward by the temporary market impact — the immediate price concession needed to absorb the flow against the current order book:

Ptexec=St−h(vt)P_t^{\text{exec}} = S_t - h(v_t)Ptexec​=St​−h(vt​)
(3)

where h(v)≥0h(v) \geq 0h(v)≥0 is the temporary impact function. The key modelling choice, motivated in chapter Execution fundamentals, is the linear temporary impact model:

h(v)=ηvh(v) = \eta vh(v)=ηv
(4)

where η>0\eta > 0η>0 is the temporary impact coefficient (units: price per trading rate). This means the execution price is depressed by ηvt\eta v_tηvt​ relative to the prevailing mid-price, in addition to the permanent depression already reflected in StS_tSt​. The temporary impact is transient: it disappears as soon as the order flow stops.

The two-component linear model (linear permanent g(v)=γvg(v) = \gamma vg(v)=γv and linear temporary h(v)=ηvh(v) = \eta vh(v)=ηv) is less empirically accurate than the square-root model for large orders but is the standard in theoretical work because it yields analytical closed-form solutions. It is the model used by Almgren and Chriss Almgren & Chriss, 2000 and Bertsimas and Lo Bertsimas & Lo, 1998.

Cost functional: implementation shortfall¶

The total proceeds from selling XXX shares are:

Π=∫0TvtPtexec dt=∫0Tvt(St−h(vt)) dt\Pi = \int_0^T v_t P_t^{\text{exec}} \, dt = \int_0^T v_t (S_t - h(v_t)) \, dtΠ=∫0T​vt​Ptexec​dt=∫0T​vt​(St​−h(vt​))dt
(5)

The implementation shortfall (IS) — the cost of execution relative to the paper portfolio value at the arrival price S0S_0S0​ — is:

IS=XS0−Π=XS0−∫0Tvt(St−h(vt)) dtIS = X S_0 - \Pi = X S_0 - \int_0^T v_t (S_t - h(v_t)) \, dtIS=XS0​−Π=XS0​−∫0T​vt​(St​−h(vt​))dt
(6)

Since St=S0+σWt−γ∫0tvs dsS_t = S_0 + \sigma W_t - \gamma \int_0^t v_s \, dsSt​=S0​+σWt​−γ∫0t​vs​ds, we can write St−S0=σWt−γ∫0tvs dsS_t - S_0 = \sigma W_t - \gamma \int_0^t v_s \, dsSt​−S0​=σWt​−γ∫0t​vs​ds, so:

IS=∫0Tvt[(S0−St)+h(vt)]dt=∫0Tvt[γ∫0tvs ds−σWt+ηvt]dtIS = \int_0^T v_t \left[(S_0 - S_t) + h(v_t)\right] dt = \int_0^T v_t \left[\gamma \int_0^t v_s \, ds - \sigma W_t + \eta v_t\right] dtIS=∫0T​vt​[(S0​−St​)+h(vt​)]dt=∫0T​vt​[γ∫0t​vs​ds−σWt​+ηvt​]dt
(7)

The IS is a random variable whose distribution depends on the price path. The objective is to choose the trading schedule {vt}0≤t≤T\{v_t\}_{0 \leq t \leq T}{vt​}0≤t≤T​ to minimise a risk-adjusted expected cost. Following Almgren and Chriss Almgren & Chriss, 2000, the objective is the mean–variance combination:

min⁡vt: ∫0Tvtdt=X, vt≥0E[IS]+λ Var[IS]\min_{v_t: \, \int_0^T v_t dt = X, \, v_t \geq 0} \mathbb{E}[IS] + \lambda \, \text{Var}[IS]vt​:∫0T​vt​dt=X,vt​≥0min​E[IS]+λVar[IS]
(8)

where λ≥0\lambda \geq 0λ≥0 is the risk-aversion parameter. This corresponds to minimising the expected cost of a risk-averse agent with CARA utility, as shown in Almgren & Chriss, 2000.

The Almgren–Chriss model¶

Expected implementation shortfall¶

Using the linear permanent impact g(v)=γvg(v) = \gamma vg(v)=γv and linear temporary impact h(v)=ηvh(v) = \eta vh(v)=ηv, the expected IS can be computed explicitly. First, integrating by parts:

∫0Tvtγ∫0tvs ds dt=γ2(∫0Tvt dt)2=γX22\int_0^T v_t \gamma \int_0^t v_s \, ds \, dt = \frac{\gamma}{2} \left(\int_0^T v_t \, dt\right)^2 = \frac{\gamma X^2}{2}∫0T​vt​γ∫0t​vs​dsdt=2γ​(∫0T​vt​dt)2=2γX2​
(9)

This shows that the permanent impact cost γ2X2\frac{\gamma}{2} X^22γ​X2 is path-independent for linear permanent impact: it equals the same constant regardless of how the order is scheduled. This is a key property of linear permanent impact that makes the optimisation tractable — only the temporary impact term and the variance term depend on the schedule.

Taking expectations of the IS (the Brownian term σWt\sigma W_tσWt​ has zero mean):

E[IS]=η∫0Tvt2 dt+γX22\mathbb{E}[IS] = \eta \int_0^T v_t^2 \, dt + \frac{\gamma X^2}{2}E[IS]=η∫0T​vt2​dt+2γX2​
(10)

The first term is the expected temporary impact cost, which is minimised by spreading the order as slowly as possible (reducing vt2v_t^2vt2​ by smoothing). The second term is fixed.

Variance of implementation shortfall¶

The stochastic part of the IS arises from the Brownian term −σ∫0TvtWt dt-\sigma \int_0^T v_t W_t \, dt−σ∫0T​vt​Wt​dt. The variance of the IS is:

Var[IS]=σ2 Var[∫0TvtWt dt]\text{Var}[IS] = \sigma^2 \, \text{Var}\left[\int_0^T v_t W_t \, dt\right]Var[IS]=σ2Var[∫0T​vt​Wt​dt]
(11)

Using the stochastic integral result Var[∫0Tf(t)Wt dt]=∫0T(∫0Tf(s)min⁡(s,t) ds)dt\text{Var}[\int_0^T f(t) W_t \, dt] = \int_0^T \left(\int_0^T f(s) \min(s,t) \, ds\right) dtVar[∫0T​f(t)Wt​dt]=∫0T​(∫0T​f(s)min(s,t)ds)dt and integration by parts:

Var[IS]=σ2∫0Txt2 dt\text{Var}[IS] = \sigma^2 \int_0^T x_t^2 \, dtVar[IS]=σ2∫0T​xt2​dt
(12)

This has a natural interpretation: the variance of execution cost is proportional to the sum of squared inventory exposures xt2x_t^2xt2​. Holding a large unexecuted inventory for a long time exposes the trader to large timing risk; reducing the inventory quickly cuts this exposure at the cost of higher impact.

The mean–variance objective¶

Since the permanent impact term γ2X2\frac{\gamma}{2} X^22γ​X2 is constant across strategies, the mean–variance objective reduces to:

min⁡x: x0=X, xT=0{η∫0Tx˙t2 dt+λσ2∫0Txt2 dt}+γX22\min_{x: \, x_0 = X, \, x_T = 0} \left\{\eta \int_0^T \dot{x}_t^2 \, dt + \lambda \sigma^2 \int_0^T x_t^2 \, dt\right\} + \frac{\gamma X^2}{2}x:x0​=X,xT​=0min​{η∫0T​x˙t2​dt+λσ2∫0T​xt2​dt}+2γX2​
(13)

where we have written vt=−x˙tv_t = -\dot{x}_tvt​=−x˙t​. This is a deterministic variational problem in the trajectory xtx_txt​: minimise a functional of the form ∫0TL(x,x˙) dt\int_0^T L(x, \dot{x}) \, dt∫0T​L(x,x˙)dt subject to fixed boundary conditions x0=Xx_0 = Xx0​=X and xT=0x_T = 0xT​=0, where:

L(x,x˙)=ηx˙2+λσ2x2L(x, \dot{x}) = \eta \dot{x}^2 + \lambda \sigma^2 x^2L(x,x˙)=ηx˙2+λσ2x2
(14)

The stochastic nature of the problem has been fully absorbed into the variance term σ2∫0Txt2 dt\sigma^2 \int_0^T x_t^2 \, dtσ2∫0T​xt2​dt, leaving a classical calculus-of-variations problem amenable to the Euler–Lagrange approach.

Optimal trajectory¶

Applying the Euler–Lagrange equation from chapter Stochastic Optimal Control (section The variational approach) to the Lagrangian L(x,x˙)=ηx˙2+λσ2x2L(x, \dot{x}) = \eta \dot{x}^2 + \lambda\sigma^2 x^2L(x,x˙)=ηx˙2+λσ2x2:

∂L∂x−ddt∂L∂x˙=2λσ2xt−2ηx¨t=0\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} = 2\lambda\sigma^2 x_t - 2\eta \ddot{x}_t = 0∂x∂L​−dtd​∂x˙∂L​=2λσ2xt​−2ηx¨t​=0
(15)

This yields the second-order linear ODE:

x¨t=κ2xt,κ=λσ2η\ddot{x}_t = \kappa^2 x_t, \quad \kappa = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda\sigma^2}{\eta}}x¨t​=κ2xt​,κ=ηλσ2​​
(16)

with boundary conditions x0=Xx_0 = Xx0​=X and xT=0x_T = 0xT​=0. The general solution is xt=Asinh⁡(κt)+Bcosh⁡(κt)x_t = A \sinh(\kappa t) + B \cosh(\kappa t)xt​=Asinh(κt)+Bcosh(κt). Applying boundary conditions:

  • x0=Xx_0 = Xx0​=X: B=XB = XB=X

  • xT=0x_T = 0xT​=0: Asinh⁡(κT)+Xcosh⁡(κT)=0⇒A=−Xcosh⁡(κT)/sinh⁡(κT)A \sinh(\kappa T) + X \cosh(\kappa T) = 0 \Rightarrow A = -X \cosh(\kappa T)/\sinh(\kappa T)Asinh(κT)+Xcosh(κT)=0⇒A=−Xcosh(κT)/sinh(κT)

Substituting and simplifying using the hyperbolic identity sinh⁡(a−b)=sinh⁡acosh⁡b−cosh⁡asinh⁡b\sinh(a-b) = \sinh a \cosh b - \cosh a \sinh bsinh(a−b)=sinhacoshb−coshasinhb:

xt∗=X sinh⁡(κ(T−t))sinh⁡(κT)\boxed{x_t^* = X \, \frac{\sinh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)}}xt∗​=Xsinh(κT)sinh(κ(T−t))​​
(17)

The optimal trading rate is:

vt∗=−x˙t∗=κX cosh⁡(κ(T−t))sinh⁡(κT)v_t^* = -\dot{x}_t^* = \kappa X \, \frac{\cosh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)}vt∗​=−x˙t∗​=κXsinh(κT)cosh(κ(T−t))​
(18)

This is a monotonically decreasing function of time: the strategy sells most aggressively at t=0t = 0t=0 and tapers towards TTT. The degree of front-loading is governed by κ=λσ2/η\kappa = \sqrt{\lambda\sigma^2/\eta}κ=λσ2/η​: higher risk aversion (larger λ\lambdaλ) or higher volatility (larger σ\sigmaσ) relative to temporary impact cost (smaller η\etaη) produces more aggressive front-loading.

Properties of the optimal solution¶

Risk-neutral limit (λ→0\lambda \to 0λ→0, κ→0\kappa \to 0κ→0): Using sinh⁡(κ(T−t))/sinh⁡(κT)→(T−t)/T\sinh(\kappa(T-t)) / \sinh(\kappa T) \to (T-t)/Tsinh(κ(T−t))/sinh(κT)→(T−t)/T as κ→0\kappa \to 0κ→0, the optimal trajectory becomes:

xt∗→X(1−tT)⇒vt∗→XTx_t^* \to X\left(1 - \frac{t}{T}\right) \quad \Rightarrow \quad v_t^* \to \frac{X}{T}xt∗​→X(1−Tt​)⇒vt∗​→TX​
(19)

This is the TWAP schedule: sell at a constant rate X/TX/TX/T throughout the horizon. The risk-neutral agent cares only about expected impact and not timing risk, and the impact-minimising strategy is to distribute the order uniformly to avoid quadratically costly bursts. This recovers the Bertsimas–Lo result Bertsimas & Lo, 1998 as a special case.

Infinitely risk-averse limit (λ→∞\lambda \to \inftyλ→∞, κ→∞\kappa \to \inftyκ→∞): The optimal inventory collapses to xt∗→0x_t^* \to 0xt∗​→0 for all t>0t > 0t>0, meaning the entire order is liquidated instantaneously at t=0t = 0t=0. The trader eliminates all timing risk by accepting the maximum possible market impact.

General case: For intermediate λ\lambdaλ, the trajectory xt∗x_t^*xt∗​ is convex (the Almgren–Chriss trajectory): it decays faster than the TWAP at the start and slower near the end. The front-loading increases monotonically with λ\lambdaλ.

The figure below illustrates the Almgren–Chriss trajectory for different values of κT\kappa TκT.

The efficient frontier¶

For each risk aversion λ\lambdaλ (equivalently, each κ\kappaκ), the optimal strategy achieves a specific pair (E[IS],Var[IS])(\mathbb{E}[IS], \text{Var}[IS])(E[IS],Var[IS]). Substituting the optimal trajectory into the cost expressions:

E[IS∗]=γX22+ηκX22coth⁡ ⁣(κT2)\mathbb{E}[IS^*] = \frac{\gamma X^2}{2} + \frac{\eta \kappa X^2}{2} \coth\!\left(\frac{\kappa T}{2}\right)E[IS∗]=2γX2​+2ηκX2​coth(2κT​)
(20)
Var[IS∗]=σ2X22κcoth⁡ ⁣(κT2)[1−κT/2sinh⁡2(κT/2)]\text{Var}[IS^*] = \frac{\sigma^2 X^2}{2\kappa} \coth\!\left(\frac{\kappa T}{2}\right) \left[1 - \frac{\kappa T / 2}{\sinh^2(\kappa T/2)}\right]Var[IS∗]=2κσ2X2​coth(2κT​)[1−sinh2(κT/2)κT/2​]
(21)

A simplified and commonly used approximation for the variance uses only the leading term:

Var[IS∗]≈σ2X22κcoth⁡ ⁣(κT2)\text{Var}[IS^*] \approx \frac{\sigma^2 X^2}{2\kappa} \coth\!\left(\frac{\kappa T}{2}\right)Var[IS∗]≈2κσ2X2​coth(2κT​)
(22)

As κ\kappaκ varies from 0 to ∞\infty∞, the pair (E[IS∗],Var[IS∗])(\mathbb{E}[IS^*], \text{Var}[IS^*])(E[IS∗],Var[IS∗]) traces out a curve in the (variance, expected cost) plane — the Almgren–Chriss efficient frontier. Every point on this frontier is the optimal strategy for some risk-aversion level λ\lambdaλ; any strategy not on the frontier is dominated. The figure below shows the frontier.

The shape of the frontier has important practical implications. Moving from the TWAP point towards aggressive execution reduces variance rapidly at first (by eliminating the bulk of timing risk), but at increasing marginal cost in expected impact. This reflects the convexity of the temporary impact cost η∫0Tvt2 dt\eta \int_0^T v_t^2 \, dtη∫0T​vt2​dt in the trading rate: executing faster always costs more in impact, but the benefit in risk reduction diminishes as the inventory is already small.

Liquidation Value at Risk¶

In addition to the mean–variance efficient frontier, Almgren and Chriss Almgren & Chriss, 2000 introduce the Liquidation Value at Risk (L-VaR), defined as the worst-case implementation shortfall at a given confidence level α\alphaα:

L-VaRα=E[IS∗]+zαVar[IS∗]\text{L-VaR}_\alpha = \mathbb{E}[IS^*] + z_\alpha \sqrt{\text{Var}[IS^*]}L-VaRα​=E[IS∗]+zα​Var[IS∗]​
(23)

where zαz_\alphazα​ is the α\alphaα-quantile of the standard normal distribution. L-VaR provides a risk measure compatible with Value-at-Risk frameworks used in risk management. Minimising L-VaR for a given α\alphaα corresponds to choosing a specific risk aversion λ=zα/(2Var[IS∗])\lambda = z_\alpha / (2\sqrt{\text{Var}[IS^*]})λ=zα​/(2Var[IS∗]​), which gives an endogenous way to calibrate λ\lambdaλ from a risk budget constraint.

Discrete-time implementation¶

In practice, the continuous-time trajectory is discretised into NNN time intervals of length τ=T/N\tau = T/Nτ=T/N. The agent sells nkn_knk​ shares in interval kkk (k=1,…,Nk = 1, \ldots, Nk=1,…,N), with remaining inventory xk=X−∑j=1k−1njx_k = X - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} n_jxk​=X−∑j=1k−1​nj​. The discrete analogue of the mean–variance objective is:

min⁡{nk}{ητ∑k=1Nnk2+λσ2τ∑k=1Nxk2}+γX22\min_{\{n_k\}} \left\{\frac{\eta}{\tau} \sum_{k=1}^N n_k^2 + \lambda \sigma^2 \tau \sum_{k=1}^N x_k^2\right\} + \frac{\gamma X^2}{2}{nk​}min​{τη​k=1∑N​nk2​+λσ2τk=1∑N​xk2​}+2γX2​
(24)

subject to ∑k=1Nnk=X\sum_{k=1}^N n_k = X∑k=1N​nk​=X. The optimal discrete trades satisfy the second-order linear recursion Almgren & Chriss, 2000:

nk+1=τ(λσ2τ+2η/τ)2η/τnk−nk−1n_{k+1} = \frac{\tau(\lambda\sigma^2\tau + 2\eta/\tau)}{2\eta/\tau} n_k - n_{k-1}nk+1​=2η/ττ(λσ2τ+2η/τ)​nk​−nk−1​
(25)

which is the discrete approximation of the continuous-time Euler–Lagrange equation x¨=κ2x\ddot{x} = \kappa^2 xx¨=κ2x. As τ→0\tau \to 0τ→0 with Nτ=TN\tau = TNτ=T fixed, the discrete solution converges to the continuous-time trajectory xt∗=Xsinh⁡(κ(T−t))/sinh⁡(κT)x_t^* = X \sinh(\kappa(T-t))/\sinh(\kappa T)xt∗​=Xsinh(κ(T−t))/sinh(κT).

The discrete version is what is implemented in practice. The schedule is computed once at the start of execution using current parameter estimates and then executed deterministically (the static IS algorithm). Dynamic adaptation — re-solving the optimal schedule intraday as new price and volume information arrives — is a natural extension but changes the objective and solution, as discussed in Implementation Shortfall target.

Implementation Shortfall target¶

Risk-neutral optimality: the Bertsimas–Lo result¶

Bertsimas and Lo Bertsimas & Lo, 1998 derive the optimal execution strategy using dynamic programming in discrete time with a purely risk-neutral objective (λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0 in the mean–variance framework). Their model uses the price dynamics Sk=Sk−1+θnk−1+ϵkS_{k} = S_{k-1} + \theta n_{k-1} + \epsilon_kSk​=Sk−1​+θnk−1​+ϵk​, where θ\thetaθ is the permanent impact coefficient and ϵk\epsilon_kϵk​ are i.i.d. zero-mean shocks.

The value function for the problem of maximising expected execution proceeds has the quadratic form Vk(xk,Sk)=akxk2+bkxkSk+ckV_k(x_k, S_k) = a_k x_k^2 + b_k x_k S_k + c_kVk​(xk​,Sk​)=ak​xk2​+bk​xk​Sk​+ck​, where the coefficients {ak,bk,ck}\{a_k, b_k, c_k\}{ak​,bk​,ck​} satisfy backward recursions. The optimal policy at each step is:

nk∗=xkN−k+1n_k^* = \frac{x_k}{N - k + 1}nk∗​=N−k+1xk​​
(26)

This is the TWAP schedule: at each step, sell an equal fraction of the remaining inventory. The result is consistent with the Almgren–Chriss λ→0\lambda \to 0λ→0 limit and establishes TWAP as the optimal IS-minimising strategy under linear permanent and temporary impact with i.i.d. price innovations.

When the price process has predictable components (non-zero expected returns), the optimal strategy departs from TWAP. Bertsimas and Lo show that with a linear return predictor μ^k\hat{\mu}_kμ^​k​ (observable at time kkk), the optimal policy takes the form:

nk∗=xkN−k+1+ϕkμ^kn_k^* = \frac{x_k}{N - k + 1} + \phi_k \hat{\mu}_knk∗​=N−k+1xk​​+ϕk​μ^​k​
(27)

where ϕk\phi_kϕk​ are coefficients that increase the trade size when the price is expected to fall (for a sell order) and reduce it when the price is expected to rise. This signal-adaptive execution is a direct generalisation of TWAP that incorporates short-horizon alpha signals into the execution decision — an important consideration for systematic strategies where residual alpha is present during execution.

Risk aversion and front-loading¶

The key insight of the Almgren–Chriss model Almgren & Chriss, 2000 is that a risk-averse trader does not implement TWAP even when returns are unpredictable. The optimal IS strategy for λ>0\lambda > 0λ>0 front-loads execution relative to TWAP, sacrificing expected cost to reduce the variance exposure from holding large inventory in a volatile market.

The degree of front-loading can be quantified by comparing the initial sell rate to the TWAP rate:

v0∗X/T=κT/sinh⁡(κT)tanh⁡(κT/2)/(κT/2)=κTcoth⁡(κT)\frac{v_0^*}{X/T} = \frac{\kappa T / \sinh(\kappa T)}{\tanh(\kappa T/2) / (\kappa T/2)} = \kappa T \coth(\kappa T)X/Tv0∗​​=tanh(κT/2)/(κT/2)κT/sinh(κT)​=κTcoth(κT)
(28)

For κT=1\kappa T = 1κT=1, the initial rate is about 1.31 times the TWAP rate; for κT=2\kappa T = 2κT=2, about 1.93 times. This front-loading effect is consistent with the practical behaviour of IS algorithms in equities, which typically execute 30–60% of the order in the first third of the scheduled window.

The IS algorithm in practice¶

In a production IS algorithm, the continuous-time trajectory is pre-computed at launch and then executed via the tactics layer (chapter Execution Tactics). The key parameters required are:

  • Volatility σ\sigmaσ: estimated from recent realised or implied volatility, typically at the intraday time scale of the execution window.

  • Temporary impact coefficient η\etaη: estimated from execution data, typically calibrated using the square-root model as η≈Yσ/V\eta \approx Y \sigma / \sqrt{V}η≈Yσ/V​ where VVV is average daily volume and YYY a market-specific constant.

  • Risk aversion λ\lambdaλ: set by the institution’s risk tolerance, either directly or derived from an L-VaR target. A common practice is to parametrise λ\lambdaλ through the execution horizon TTT, which is set by specifying a participation rate — a target fraction of market volume — and using the predicted total volume to derive the horizon.

The IS algorithm is inherently static: the schedule is computed once from current parameter estimates. Dynamic variants re-solve the optimal schedule at each time step using updated estimates of volatility and the remaining horizon, trading additional computation for improved adaptation.

VWAP target¶

IS and VWAP under volume-proportional impact¶

Under certain conditions, the VWAP-optimal strategy coincides with the IS-optimal strategy. Kato (2017) shows that when the market impact of trading is proportional to the fraction of market volume traded — h(vt)=ηvt/Vth(v_t) = \eta v_t / V_th(vt​)=ηvt​/Vt​, where VtV_tVt​ is the market trading rate — the risk-neutral IS-optimal strategy is to trade proportionally to the market volume profile. This is the static VWAP schedule: vt∗=(X/VT)Vtv_t^* = (X / V_T) V_tvt∗​=(X/VT​)Vt​, where VT=∫0TVt dtV_T = \int_0^T V_t \, dtVT​=∫0T​Vt​dt is the total market volume. The two benchmarks therefore share the same optimal strategy under the natural assumption that temporary impact is proportional to participation rate.

In practice, the two targets differ when impact deviates from this proportional form and particularly when timing risk is relevant: VWAP is agnostic to the trader’s risk aversion, while IS front-loading reflects the risk of adverse price movements. The VWAP target is more appropriate for agency execution where the goal is to blend into market flow, while IS is more appropriate for proprietary execution where the investor bears timing risk directly.

Static VWAP schedule¶

The simplest VWAP strategy is the static schedule: at time 0, estimate the daily volume profile mt=Vt/VTm_t = V_t / V_Tmt​=Vt​/VT​ from historical data, and allocate the order proportionally:

vt=X⋅mtv_t = X \cdot m_tvt​=X⋅mt​
(29)

so that the participation rate vt/Vt=X/VTv_t / V_t = X / V_Tvt​/Vt​=X/VT​ is constant across all time bins. The static schedule perfectly tracks VWAP if the realised volume profile matches the forecast; its tracking error arises from deviations between actual and predicted volume.

Volume profiles exhibit strong intraday patterns — the well-known U-shape — that are stable on average but noisy on any given day. The key sources of volume forecast uncertainty are:

  • Total daily volume: the aggregate number of shares traded that day, which can deviate significantly from its historical average on news or macro event days.

  • Intraday distribution: the shape of the volume curve within the day, which can shift due to scheduled economic releases, index rebalancing flows, or other events.

Dynamic VWAP: the Busseti–Boyd framework¶

Busseti & Boyd (2015) cast the VWAP tracking problem as a Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control (LQSC) problem (chapter Stochastic Optimal Control, section Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control) and derive a dynamic strategy that adapts the execution schedule as volume information is revealed intraday.

Setup: the trading period is divided into MMM bins of equal length. Let qnq_nqn​ be the number of shares executed in bin nnn, vnv_nvn​ the market volume in bin nnn (random), VM=∑n=0M−1vnV_M = \sum_{n=0}^{M-1} v_nVM​=∑n=0M−1​vn​ the total daily volume, and mn=vn/VMm_n = v_n / V_Mmn​=vn​/VM​ the realised volume fraction. The VWAP slippage relative to the market VWAP is:

S=∑n=0M−1qnpn−Π⋅pvwapΠ⋅pvwapS = \frac{\sum_{n=0}^{M-1} q_n p_n - \Pi \cdot p_{\text{vwap}}}{\Pi \cdot p_{\text{vwap}}}S=Π⋅pvwap​∑n=0M−1​qn​pn​−Π⋅pvwap​​
(30)

where pnp_npn​ is the mid-price in bin nnn and Π\PiΠ is the total order size. Neglecting market impact and using a driftless geometric random walk for prices, the expected slippage is zero and the variance simplifies to:

Var[S]=∑n=1M−1σn2 E0 ⁣[(VnVM−QnΠ)2]\text{Var}[S] = \sum_{n=1}^{M-1} \sigma_n^2 \, \mathbb{E}_0\!\left[\left(\frac{V_n}{V_M} - \frac{Q_n}{\Pi}\right)^2\right]Var[S]=n=1∑M−1​σn2​E0​[(VM​Vn​​−ΠQn​​)2]
(31)

where Vn=∑j<nvjV_n = \sum_{j<n} v_jVn​=∑j<n​vj​ is the cumulative market volume, Qn=∑j<nqjQ_n = \sum_{j<n} q_jQn​=∑j<n​qj​ is the cumulative executed quantity, and σn\sigma_nσn​ is the per-bin price volatility. The objective min⁡{qn}Var[S]\min_{\{q_n\}} \text{Var}[S]min{qn​}​Var[S] is quadratic in qnq_nqn​, fitting the LQSC structure.

State space: the state vector is xn=(Qn,Vn)Tx_n = (Q_n, V_n)^Txn​=(Qn​,Vn​)T, combining the cumulative executed quantity and the cumulative market volume. The state dynamics are xn+1=xn+(qn,vn)Tx_{n+1} = x_n + (q_n, v_n)^Txn+1​=xn​+(qn​,vn​)T, which is linear in the control qnq_nqn​ and the noise vnv_nvn​.

Riccati solution: since the cost is quadratic in the state and the dynamics are linear, the LQSC backward recursion from chapter Stochastic Optimal Control applies. The optimal control at each step is affine in the current state:

qn∗=Knxn+ℓnq_n^* = K_n x_n + \ell_nqn∗​=Kn​xn​+ℓn​
(32)

where the gains KnK_nKn​ and ℓn\ell_nℓn​ are computed backwards from the terminal condition via Riccati equations. The resulting dynamic VWAP strategy is:

qn∗=Π⋅Vn+En[vn]En[VM]−Qn\boxed{q_n^* = \Pi \cdot \frac{V_n + \mathbb{E}_n[v_n]}{\mathbb{E}_n[V_M]} - Q_n}qn∗​=Π⋅En​[VM​]Vn​+En​[vn​]​−Qn​​
(33)

This elegant formula has a direct interpretation: at each bin nnn, compute the expected total market volume En[VM]\mathbb{E}_n[V_M]En​[VM​] (updated using all information available through bin n−1n-1n−1), determine what fraction of Π\PiΠ should have been executed by the end of bin nnn to track the VWAP exactly, and execute the difference between that target and what has actually been executed so far. The strategy thus corrects for cumulative volume forecast errors one bin at a time, catching up all accumulated deviations immediately at the next opportunity.

Static fallback: if no intraday information is used (only the information available at n=0n=0n=0), the optimal strategy reduces to:

qnstatic=Π⋅E0[vn]E0[VM]q_n^{\text{static}} = \Pi \cdot \frac{\mathbb{E}_0[v_n]}{\mathbb{E}_0[V_M]}qnstatic​=Π⋅E0​[VM​]E0​[vn​]​
(34)

the proportional static schedule where the allocation to each bin is the predicted fraction of daily volume. This is the static VWAP schedule from the previous section.

Performance: Busseti and Boyd report that the dynamic strategy reduces VWAP tracking error (root mean squared slippage) by approximately 10% relative to the static schedule on a sample of DJIA stocks, with execution cost savings of approximately 50ona50 on a 50ona1 million order.

Volume modelling¶

The quality of the dynamic VWAP strategy depends critically on the quality of the volume forecasts En[vn]\mathbb{E}_n[v_n]En​[vn​] and En[VM]\mathbb{E}_n[V_M]En​[VM​]. Busseti & Boyd (2015) model the intraday volume profile (m0,…,mM−1)(m_0, \ldots, m_{M-1})(m0​,…,mM−1​) as a multivariate log-normal distribution, capturing:

  • Intraday seasonality: the U-shaped average volume profile, which concentrates at the open and close.

  • Stock-specific scaling: each stock has a characteristic volume level captured by a stock-specific factor.

  • Cross-bin correlations: volume is correlated across adjacent bins (high volume in one bin predicts higher volume in the next), captured by a low-rank plus banded covariance matrix.

Given partial observations of the realised volume through bin n−1n-1n−1, the conditional distribution of the remaining volume profile follows a log-normal distribution whose parameters are updated via standard conditional Gaussian formulas (Schur complement). The required expectations En[vτ]\mathbb{E}_n[v_\tau]En​[vτ​] and En[VM]\mathbb{E}_n[V_M]En​[VM​] are computed as log-normal moments using these updated parameters.

In practice, volume models are calibrated from 20–60 days of historical intraday data, discriminating by features such as day of the week, expiration dates, and macro announcement calendars to avoid mixing volume patterns from structurally different days.

Portfolio execution¶

Multi-asset extension¶

Consider simultaneously executing orders in ddd assets, with target sizes X(i)X^{(i)}X(i) for i=1,…,di = 1, \ldots, di=1,…,d. The state is now a vector xt=(xt(1),…,xt(d))T\mathbf{x}_t = (x_t^{(1)}, \ldots, x_t^{(d)})^Txt​=(xt(1)​,…,xt(d)​)T of remaining inventories and the control is the vector of trading rates vt=(vt(1),…,vt(d))T\mathbf{v}_t = (v_t^{(1)}, \ldots, v_t^{(d)})^Tvt​=(vt(1)​,…,vt(d)​)T.

Asset prices evolve as a multivariate arithmetic Brownian motion with cross-impact:

dSt(i)=σ(i)dWt(i)−∑jgijvt(j) dtdS_t^{(i)} = \sigma^{(i)} dW_t^{(i)} - \sum_j g_{ij} v_t^{(j)} \, dtdSt(i)​=σ(i)dWt(i)​−j∑​gij​vt(j)​dt
(35)

where G=(gij)G = (g_{ij})G=(gij​) is the cross-permanent-impact matrix: selling asset jjj at rate vt(j)v_t^{(j)}vt(j)​ moves the price of asset iii by gijvt(j)g_{ij} v_t^{(j)}gij​vt(j)​. The Wiener processes Wt(i)W_t^{(i)}Wt(i)​ are correlated with instantaneous correlation ρij\rho_{ij}ρij​, giving the covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ with Σij=ρijσ(i)σ(j)\Sigma_{ij} = \rho_{ij} \sigma^{(i)} \sigma^{(j)}Σij​=ρij​σ(i)σ(j).

The execution price for asset iii is:

Pt(i),exec=St(i)−hiivt(i)P_t^{(i),\text{exec}} = S_t^{(i)} - h_{ii} v_t^{(i)}Pt(i),exec​=St(i)​−hii​vt(i)​
(36)

where temporary impact is assumed diagonal (each asset’s temporary impact depends only on its own trading rate; cross-asset temporary effects are typically negligible at practical order sizes).

Portfolio cost functional¶

The multi-asset mean–variance objective is:

min⁡vt{E[ISportfolio]+λ2Var[ISportfolio]}\min_{\mathbf{v}_t} \left\{\mathbb{E}[IS_{\text{portfolio}}] + \frac{\lambda}{2} \text{Var}[IS_{\text{portfolio}}]\right\}vt​min​{E[ISportfolio​]+2λ​Var[ISportfolio​]}
(37)

where ISportfolio=∑i=1d(X(i)S0(i)−∫0Tvt(i)Pt(i),exec dt)IS_{\text{portfolio}} = \sum_{i=1}^d \left(X^{(i)} S_0^{(i)} - \int_0^T v_t^{(i)} P_t^{(i),\text{exec}} \, dt\right)ISportfolio​=∑i=1d​(X(i)S0(i)​−∫0T​vt(i)​Pt(i),exec​dt).

The expected cost separates into asset-specific temporary impact costs plus a path-independent permanent impact term 12XTGX\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{X}^T G \mathbf{X}21​XTGX. The variance of cost is:

Var[ISportfolio]=∫0TxtTΣ xt dt\text{Var}[IS_{\text{portfolio}}] = \int_0^T \mathbf{x}_t^T \Sigma \, \mathbf{x}_t \, dtVar[ISportfolio​]=∫0T​xtT​Σxt​dt
(38)

This is the key cross-asset term: the variance of the portfolio’s execution cost depends on the joint inventory trajectory through the covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ. Correlated assets contribute positively to the total variance, but can be managed jointly to reduce it.

The multi-asset mean–variance objective then reduces to:

min⁡xt: x0=X, xT=0{∫0Tx˙tTHx˙t dt+λ∫0TxtTΣ xt dt}\min_{\mathbf{x}_t: \, \mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{X}, \, \mathbf{x}_T = \mathbf{0}} \left\{\int_0^T \dot{\mathbf{x}}_t^T H \dot{\mathbf{x}}_t \, dt + \lambda \int_0^T \mathbf{x}_t^T \Sigma \, \mathbf{x}_t \, dt\right\}xt​:x0​=X,xT​=0min​{∫0T​x˙tT​Hx˙t​dt+λ∫0T​xtT​Σxt​dt}
(39)

where H=diag(η(1),…,η(d))H = \text{diag}(\eta^{(1)}, \ldots, \eta^{(d)})H=diag(η(1),…,η(d)) is the diagonal temporary impact matrix.

The matrix Euler–Lagrange equation¶

Applying the Euler–Lagrange equation to the vector Lagrangian L(x,x˙)=x˙THx˙+λxTΣxL(\mathbf{x}, \dot{\mathbf{x}}) = \dot{\mathbf{x}}^T H \dot{\mathbf{x}} + \lambda \mathbf{x}^T \Sigma \mathbf{x}L(x,x˙)=x˙THx˙+λxTΣx:

∂L∂x−ddt∂L∂x˙=2λΣxt−2Hx¨t=0\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{x}} - \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{x}}} = 2\lambda \Sigma \mathbf{x}_t - 2H \ddot{\mathbf{x}}_t = 0∂x∂L​−dtd​∂x˙∂L​=2λΣxt​−2Hx¨t​=0
(40)

giving the matrix ODE:

x¨t=K2xt,K2=λH−1Σ\ddot{\mathbf{x}}_t = K^2 \mathbf{x}_t, \quad K^2 = \lambda H^{-1} \Sigmax¨t​=K2xt​,K2=λH−1Σ
(41)

The matrix K2K^2K2 couples the trajectories of all ddd assets through the covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ and the impact matrix H−1H^{-1}H−1. The general solution involves matrix exponentials:

xt∗=sinh⁡(K(T−t))[sinh⁡(KT)]−1X\mathbf{x}_t^* = \sinh(K(T-t)) [\sinh(KT)]^{-1} \mathbf{X}xt∗​=sinh(K(T−t))[sinh(KT)]−1X
(42)

where the matrix K=λH−1ΣK = \sqrt{\lambda H^{-1} \Sigma}K=λH−1Σ​ (principal square root of the positive semi-definite matrix λH−1Σ\lambda H^{-1} \SigmaλH−1Σ) can be computed via eigendecomposition of H−1ΣH^{-1} \SigmaH−1Σ.

For practical implementation, the matrix ODE is solved numerically on a discrete grid using either the matrix exponential or forward Euler integration of the first-order system.

Natural hedging during execution¶

The coupling through Σ\SigmaΣ has an important economic interpretation: correlated assets should be liquidated jointly. If two assets have positive correlation (ρ>0\rho > 0ρ>0), selling both simultaneously is better than selling them sequentially, because the price risk of holding residual inventory in one asset is partially hedged by the comovement with the other.

More precisely, consider two perfectly correlated assets (ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1, σ(1)=σ(2)=σ\sigma^{(1)} = \sigma^{(2)} = \sigmaσ(1)=σ(2)=σ, η(1)=η(2)=η\eta^{(1)} = \eta^{(2)} = \etaη(1)=η(2)=η). The joint portfolio trajectory X(1)xt(1)+X(2)xt(2)X^{(1)} x_t^{(1)} + X^{(2)} x_t^{(2)}X(1)xt(1)​+X(2)xt(2)​ is perfectly hedged against price movements as long as the two inventory trajectories track each other proportionally — if one asset’s price moves adversely, the other’s moves identically. The optimal strategy therefore schedules both assets with identical normalised trajectories, and the portfolio execution cost is no higher than executing either asset alone.

For imperfectly correlated assets (0<ρ<10 < \rho < 10<ρ<1), partial hedging is still possible: the optimal joint trajectory front-loads the more volatile asset and holds the less volatile one longer, exploiting the natural hedge to reduce total variance at lower impact cost.

Proxy instruments¶

A powerful extension of multi-asset portfolio execution is the use of proxy instruments: highly liquid instruments that are correlated with the portfolio but not themselves in the target portfolio (e.g. index futures for a basket of equities). A proxy instrument can be traded at low cost and high liquidity to hedge the portfolio’s price risk during execution, effectively extending the execution window without increasing timing risk.

In the framework above, proxy instruments enter the optimisation with boundary conditions x0(proxy)=0x_0^{(\text{proxy})} = 0x0(proxy)​=0 and xT(proxy)=0x_T^{(\text{proxy})} = 0xT(proxy)​=0: they carry no net position change but can be used as intermediaries to reduce portfolio-level risk during the execution window. The optimizer freely uses them as they appear in the covariance matrix Σ\SigmaΣ and their use is only constrained by their boundary conditions. This allows the algorithm to temporarily take on a proxy position to hedge inventory risk, then unwind it as the primary positions are completed.
